forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Leicester's auditor closes its medium-term finance recommendation as council drops exceptional support plans
news_drafts.lead:
Leicester City Council no longer expects to need exceptional financial support in the foreseeable future, according to a draft annual audit report on its 2025/26 accounts. Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. The report goes to the council's Governance and Audit Committee on 18 November 2026.

The report, dated 6 November 2026, says: "Due to the significantly improved financial position, the Council no longer envisages requiring exceptional financial support (EFS) in the foreseeable future."

The council's external auditor says that, because of the improved position, it does not consider there to be a significant weakness in the council's arrangements to address its medium-term financial challenge in 2025/26. It has also closed the key recommendation it made on the subject in the prior year. The draft report gives no figures for the improvement.

findings.headline: The paper says Leicester's settlement produced a forecast change in Core Spending Power of 36.1% over 2024/25 to 2028/29, which is greater than the unitary authority average.
findings.detail: The paper notes the settlement distributed funding using the new 'Fair Funding Review 2.0' formulas, and that the increase is larger for cities with high deprivation. It also says core spending power in England remains roughly 9% below 2010/11 levels in real terms.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how the new funding formulas have changed their own core spending power.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power change 36.1% (2024/25 to 2028/29, chart label); England core spending power roughly 9% below 2010/11 levels in real terms
findings.quote: resulted in a forecast change in Core Spending Power greater than the national average for other unitary authorities

findings.headline: Reorganisation across Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland is paused for review following the Government's September 2026 announcement.
findings.detail: The paper says risks will remain once transition recommences, including managing the disaggregation of services and finances and maintaining financial systems. The Council has set aside £14m in its Budget Strategy Reserve for LGR transition costs.
findings.matters: A paused reorganisation affects the financial planning, hosting arrangements and transition costs a finance director at any council in a reorganisation area must plan for.
findings.figures: £14m set aside for LGR transition costs
findings.quote: reorganisation across Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland is currently paused for review

findings.headline: The number of procurement waivers fell from 122 in 2024/25 to 53 in 2025/26, and the contract value affected fell from £55.8 million to £10 million.
findings.detail: The auditor says the reduction indicates a positive impact from improved controls and training introduced after an internal audit review. It recommends that the Council continue to take assurance over compliance so the improvement is sustained.
findings.matters: Waiver counts and contract values are a measure of procurement control a finance director elsewhere can compare with their own contract rules.
findings.figures: waivers 122 (2024/25) to 53 (2025/26); value £55.8 million to £10 million
findings.quote: the number of waivers has reduced from 122 in 2024/25 to 53 in 2025/26 and that the value fell more significantly from £55.8 million to £10 million

findings.headline: During 2025/26, the Council settled a legal claim with its waste contractor through a £10 million settlement deed.
findings.detail: The auditor reviewed the decision-making process and found appropriate options were considered, supported by external legal and professional advice. The paper says the financial implications were reflected in the financial statements and that there was no disruption to waste collection services.
findings.matters: A £10 million settlement with a waste contractor is a contract dispute outcome a finance director elsewhere may face with their own contractors.
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council settled a legal claim following a protracted commercial dispute with its waste contractor, through a £10 million settlement deed.

findings.headline: The Regulator of Social Housing issued the Council's housing consumer standards a rating of C3, and the auditor has updated its key recommendation on housing.
findings.detail: The inspection found around 70% of properties did not have a current electrical safety test, and that the last comprehensive stock survey was in 2009. The Council has a Provider Improvement Plan and an RSH Oversight Board that meets monthly. The key recommendation remains until the Council reaches consumer standards C2 or above.
findings.matters: A C3 consumer standards rating and a key recommendation on housing compliance are a governance and regulatory risk any council with a large housing stock will want to compare against.
findings.figures: consumer standards rating C3; around 70% of properties without a current electrical safety test; last comprehensive stock survey 2009
findings.quote: issued a consumer standards rating of C3, indicating that serious failings had been identified and significant improvement was required
